profile.reading: This building sits within the footprint of the former Loring Air Force Base in Limestone, Maine, now redeveloped as the Loring Commerce Centre, a roughly 3,800 acre commercial, industrial, and aviation park built from the decommissioned base's own buildings and infrastructure. The generic name attached to this listing, simply Datacenter, gives no operator or company identity of its own. The Commerce Centre's published tenant directory lists more than twenty businesses on site, including one technology firm, Lattice Technology Group, an engineering and systems integration consultancy, but Lattice's own description of its work is consulting and architecture design rather than operating server infrastructure or leasing hosting space, and nothing ties that company specifically to this building. Former military bases like Loring often retain purpose built communications or computer rooms from their active service days, structures that sometimes continue in some IT or utility role for a redeveloped site even without becoming a commercial data center business. Given the bare generic tag and the lack of any confirmed operator name tied to this specific structure, this entry is recorded as an unconfirmed building within the Loring Commerce Centre redevelopment, most plausibly a legacy base facility repurposed for some internal IT or utility function, rather than a verified commercial data center.

reading.body:
Maine's three mapped data center facilities publish zero megawatts of confirmed capacity, and this Aroostook County building is one reason: it carries only a generic name and no operator.

The building sits within Loring Commerce Centre, a 3,800-acre redevelopment of Loring Air Force Base in Limestone. Its listing carries only the word Datacenter, no operator, and the park's directory of more than twenty tenants confirms no data center operator. The one technology-adjacent tenant, Lattice Technology Group, describes itself as a systems integration consultancy, not a hosting or colocation provider, and nothing ties it to this structure.

For AI scaling, the relevant fact is not the building but the disclosure gap. Maine has three mapped data center facilities and zero published megawatts of confirmed capacity across the state. A former military base with legacy communications or computer rooms may retain some internal IT or utility role, but without power consumption, rack density, cooling capacity, or an operator name, no capacity can be assigned and no compute claim can be made.

What this does not tell the reader is whether any server infrastructure actually operates here. The absence of published specifications does not indicate absence of infrastructure, only absence of disclosure. This entry is unconfirmed, and the state total of zero published megawatts should be read as a floor of public knowledge, not a ceiling on physical equipment.
